How to Search Public Records in Texas

Texas keeps most records at the county level. Learn which office holds court, property, and business records, and how the Texas Public Information Act and its 10-business-day rule work.

Key takeaways

  • ✓Texas records are kept by 254 counties, so find the right county office before you search.
  • ✓The Public Information Act gives a governmental body 10 business days to respond, release records, or ask the Attorney General for a ruling.
  • ✓Business filings are at the Secretary of State, while property deeds are with the county clerk and values with the appraisal district.

In this guide

  1. Business Records: the Secretary of State and the County Clerk
  2. Court Records: Start With the Right Court
  3. Property Records: Three Offices, Three Questions
  4. The Texas Public Information Act
  5. Practical Tips for Texas

Texas has 254 counties, and most of the records people look for are kept locally rather than in one statewide database. That makes the first question "which office?" before "which website?". This guide walks through business, court, and property records in Texas and explains how to use the state's open records law when a record is not already published.

Business Records: the Secretary of State and the County Clerk

Corporations, limited liability companies, and limited partnerships are registered with the Texas Secretary of State, which provides an online service called SOSDirect for searching entities and ordering documents. A record typically shows the exact legal name, entity type, filing date, status, and registered agent, and the filings often list the people who govern the company. Sole proprietors and general partnerships that operate under a trade name generally file an assumed name certificate with the county clerk instead, so a business that does not appear at the state level may still be on file in its home county.

Court Records: Start With the Right Court

Texas trial courts are split by type and size of case. Justice courts and municipal courts handle small claims, traffic, and minor offenses. County courts and district courts handle larger civil disputes and felony cases. District clerks usually keep district court records, while county clerks keep county court records, and each county sets up its own search tools. Some counties offer a free online docket search, and others charge for document images or require an account.

The Texas Judicial Branch also runs a statewide portal called re:SearchTX, which provides access to e-filed documents in participating courts. Coverage depends on the court and the type of case, so check the Texas Judicial Branch website for what is available. Federal cases in Texas are filed in one of four federal districts (Northern, Southern, Eastern, and Western) and are searched through PACER.

  • For a person with a common name, add a middle name or date of birth wherever the portal allows.
  • Texas does not have a single free statewide criminal record database for the public. The Texas Department of Public Safety offers a paid name-based search of conviction records, so check its site for the current scope and fees.
  • Search the county where the event happened, and nearby counties if you are not sure.

Property Records: Three Offices, Three Questions

  • County appraisal district: sets the appraised value and lists the owner of record and property details. Most districts have a free online search by address or owner.
  • County clerk: keeps the Official Public Records, which include recorded deeds, deeds of trust, liens, and releases.
  • County tax assessor-collector: shows current and delinquent property taxes.

Texas is often described as a "non-disclosure" state, meaning sale prices are generally not required to be reported on recorded deeds. As a result, a deed may not show what a buyer paid, and the appraisal district's value is not a sale price.

The Texas Public Information Act

The Texas Public Information Act, found in Chapter 552 of the Government Code, is the state's open records law, and the Office of the Attorney General publishes guidance for requesters. A request should be in writing and sent to the governmental body's public information officer. No special form is required, and the clock starts when the written request reaches the right office.

  1. Within 10 business days, the governmental body must do one of several things: release the information, tell you when it will be available, tell you it has none, send an itemized cost estimate, or ask the Attorney General for a ruling because it believes an exception applies.
  2. If it asks for a ruling, the Attorney General generally has 45 business days to decide, and it can take an additional 10 business days.
  3. If a body fails to respond or fails to request a ruling within 10 business days, you can contact the Open Records Division of the Attorney General's office for help.

Agencies may charge for copies and labor in some cases, and you can narrow a request to lower the cost. Many governmental bodies, including large counties and school districts, now take requests through online portals.

Practical Tips for Texas

  • Identify the county first. Because records are local, the same company can have an assumed name filing in one county and a state registration in Austin.
  • Use "business days" when you count. Weekends and designated non-business days for the agency do not count.
  • Save the date you sent a written request. It is the starting point for every deadline.
  • For a certified copy of a court or land record, contact the clerk who holds the original.

Office names, portals, and fees change, so confirm details with the office that holds the record before you rely on them. For general background, our guides on county offices, property records, and public records requests explain these concepts in more detail.
